about: Duiblinn (Dublin): the church by the black pool and the ford of hurdles (to 841), the heathens' ship-fort and its kings (841 to 902), the empty years (902 to 917) and Dyflin, the town of plots and plank paths (917 to 1066). Written 6 Oct 2026 from Design/content/dossiers/duiblinn.md, Design/content/realms/irish_sea.md, Design/content/peoples/irish_gaelic.md and the spine. A draft in the game's own files, for the user to overwrite. (?) marks what is not verified. Woven with the region on 7 Oct 2026: King Cerball of Leinster and Sitriuc Cáech made real; Amlaíb Cuarán moved here from hi.json as one person; ties run both ways, beats pointed at their cards (Data/encounters/northumbria_irish_sea_793.json).

ports.summary: In 793 this is a church in a ring bank beside a dark pool, and a village of farmers and fishermen at a ford of hurdles a short walk up the river. There is no town, no coin, no toll and no market: a stranger from over the sea trades only as the guest of the man who keeps the church's land, who takes a gift and the first choice. A merchant comes with wine and salt for hides and wool cloaks, and comes back because somebody at the ford knows his boat.
ports.seasons: The cattle go to the hill pastures at the start of May and come home at the start of November, when the slaughter fills the strand with hides and the food-rents fall due. The fairs are inland at the start of August, and in the heathens' years the captives come in at the leaves' fall, after the raiding. Every winter gale moves the bar in the bay, so the way in is learned again each spring.

history.text: Siadal, abbot of Duiblinn, died (the Four Masters give it under 785; it may be as late as 790). No abbot or bishop of the house is named after him.
history.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Dublin_to_795; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Scandinavian_Dublin. The Annals of the Four Masters were not opened (?)

history.text: Máel Ruain of Tallaght, 'bishop and soldier of Christ', died on the seventh of July. Airerán followed him.
Bran Ardchenn, king of Leinster, was burned in a house with his queen by Fínsnechta, who was king after him. The same year: 'The burning of Rechru by the heathens.'
The heathens burned the island off Skerries, took the cattle-tribute and broke the shrine.
Áed son of Niall, king of Tara, wasted Leinster twice in one month.
Cellach, abbot of Iona, began the new house of Columba at Kells, after sixty-eight of his community were killed in 806. The church there was finished in 814.
The community of Tallaght stopped the fair of Tailtiu, so that neither horse nor chariot ran.
history.source: Annals of Ulster 811, from memory (?); the spine's calendar notes the year the fair was not held

history.text: Howth was raided and many women were carried off.
Clondalkin was plundered.
Sixty ships came on the Liffey and sixty on the Boyne.
history.source: Annals of Ulster 837.3, via Design/content/realms/irish_sea.md and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Scandinavian_Dublin

history.text: The heathens made a ship-fort at Duiblinn, and stayed the winter.
history.source: Annals of Ulster 841.4 (chronicle_793.json 841-duiblinn-longphort). Where the fort stood is not known

history.text: Swords and Finglas were raided. Turgeis was taken by Máel Sechnaill and drowned.
Máel Sechnaill plundered the fort. A hundred and forty ships of the king of the Foreigners came to the Liffey.
Dark Foreigners came to Duiblinn, beat the Fair Foreigners and wrecked the fort.
Amlaíb, son of the king of Lochlann, came to Ireland. The Foreigners gave him hostages and the Irish gave him tribute.
The kings of the Foreigners searched the old tombs on the Boyne, which had never been done before.
Amlaíb's fort at Clondalkin was burned and a hundred of his men were killed.
Amlaíb and Ímar came back to the Liffey from Dumbarton, taken after four months, with two hundred ships and a great prey of English, Britons and Picts.
history.source: Annals of Ulster 870.6, 871.2, via Design/content/realms/irish_sea.md; chronicle_793.json 870-dumbarton-taken

history.text: Ímar, king of the Northmen of all Ireland and Britain, died. A later telling says of a sudden horrible disease.
history.source: Annals of Ulster 873.3; the disease from the Fragmentary Annals, via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Scandinavian_Dublin

history.text: The Foreigners of the fort split into two parties.

The men of Leinster under Cerball and the men of Brega under Máel Finnia took the fort. The heathens were driven out, left a good number of their ships, and fled half dead to Wales, the Wirral and beyond.
Sitriuc, grandson of Ímar, came back and took the place.
Niall Glúndub, king of Tara, was killed fighting the Foreigners at the weir up the river.
history.source: Annals of Ulster 919.3, via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilmainham and Design/content/realms/irish_sea.md

history.text: Amlaíb son of Gothfrith came home from the battle in England with few ships.
The town was sacked and burned by the Irish.
The Foreigners plundered Kells and took three thousand captives, with gold, silver and cattle.
The Foreigners were beaten at Tara. Máel Sechnaill besieged the town three days and three nights, and every Irish slave in it was set free. Amlaíb Cuarán went to Iona in penitence and died there.
history.source: Annals of Tigernach 980 (chronicle_793.json 980-tara); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amla%C3%ADb_Cuar%C3%A1n. Amlaíb was not at the battle; his death may be 981

history.text: Máel Sechnaill besieged the town again. They had no water but the sea's. An ounce of gold from every plot was laid on them, to be paid each Christmas night for ever.
history.source: Annals of Tigernach 989, via Design/content/realms/irish_sea.md and lore/law_tolls.md

history.text: About this year, or two years before, King Sitriuc struck the first pennies made in Ireland, copies of King Æthelred's.
Brian and Máel Sechnaill beat the Foreigners and the Leinstermen at Glenn Máma in the last days of the year. Brian was in the town at New Year and burned Tomar's wood.
history.source: Annals of Ulster 999.8, via Design/content/realms/irish_sea.md; lore/gods_cult.md

history.text: On Good Friday, the twenty-third of April, Brian's army fought the Foreigners and the Leinstermen at Clontarf. Brian was killed. Sitriuc stayed inside and the town was not taken.
King Sitriuc went to Rome. Soon after he founded the church of the Holy Trinity, with Dúnán as its first bishop.
Sitriuc's son was taken by the king of Brega. His ransom was twelve hundred cows, six score Welsh horses, sixty ounces of gold, sixty of silver and the sword of Carlus.
history.source: Annals of Ulster 1029, via Design/content/realms/irish_sea.md; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigtrygg_Silkbeard has 140 British horses

history.text: About this year a warship of sixty oars was built here of oak. She ended on the bottom of Roskilde fjord.
Diarmait, king of Leinster, took the town and set his son Murchad over it. That winter Harold son of Godwin had been here in exile.
Murchad took tribute from the Isle of Man.

eras.text: A church in a ring bank by the pool, perhaps without an abbot since Siadal, and the ford village up the river. No coin, no toll, no market. The steward of the church's land stands for a stranger, takes a gift and first choice, and names sureties for every bargain; worth is said in cows and ounces. Rechru burns in 795 and the smoke is seen from the strand. Each summer after that the fishermen watch the mouth of the bay, and in 837 sixty ships come up the river.

A turf bank, ships drawn up inside it, and men who mean to stay till spring. The church is theirs or empty. They have captives and church silver and want grain, wine and salt, and they weigh everything. In 849 the king of Tara plunders the fort; in 851 other Foreigners come and wreck it. Nobody here can promise a merchant next year.

The fort has kings: Amlaíb, Ímar, and after 873 their quarrelling heirs. A king's man takes his share on the strand. Captives go out by the shipload, above all in 871; silver goes by weight in arm-rings and cut pieces; the dead are laid up the river with swords and scales. Irish kings fight the place, hire it and marry into it. In 893 it splits in two, and in 902 it is taken in a day.

Empty of Northmen. Hulls rot where they were left half built, the bank slumps, and cattle graze inside it. The ford village goes on as before, and so does Tallaght. There is nothing to buy but hides and nobody to pay a toll to. Men who know say the people of the fort are on Man, in the Wirral and by the Ribble, and have not forgotten the way back.

Dyflin: fenced plots along plank paths, wattle houses with a hearth and two benches, comb-makers, smiths, shoemakers and shipwrights, and a king whose kin also sit at York. An earth bank goes round it about 950. Slaves, hides, cloaks and ships go out; wine, salt, amber, walrus tooth and silk come in. It burns in 944 and is built again on the same fence lines. Old Amlaíb Cuarán is baptised and keeps poets of both tongues.

After Tara the Irish slaves walk out free and the old king goes to Iona to die. The town pays the king of Tara: cattle, and from 989 an ounce of gold from every plot each Christmas night. Sitriuc Silkbeard strikes pennies with his name on them. Brian holds the town at New Year 1000 and burns Thor's wood. No load moves on a Sunday when an Irish king's steward is looking.

Clontarf is fought within sight of the bank and the town trades the week after. Sitriuc goes to Rome and builds a wooden church of the Holy Trinity on the height, with a bishop who looks to Canterbury. The pennies grow light and stay at home. Kings change three times in ten years. About 1042 the yard lays the keel of a sixty-oar ship.

Leinster's town. Diarmait sets his son Murchad over it; the Foreigners keep their plots, their law mound and their ships, and hire both out. Harold son of Godwin wintered here and went home with crews. Man pays tribute from 1061. English exiles and Welsh kings come for fleets, and a skipper is asked whose silver he sails on.

sites.name: The black pool
sites.see: A small river widens into a still pool, dark as peat water, before it meets the brown tidal Liffey; boats lie on the mud at its lip with their sterns to the reeds. Behind is a low ridge with smoke on it, and far off to the north the long head of Benn Étair. It smells of bog water, weed and wet hide, and the only sound at low water is curlews.
sites.source: The pool where the Poddle meets the Liffey: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Dublin_to_795; Research/water_levels/ireland_isles.md. That boats lay here in 793 is the dossier's inference

sites.name: The ford of hurdles
sites.see: Woven hurdles pegged across the river bed, showing at low water as a pale crooked line from bank to bank, with a punt and a hide boat drawn up beside a round wattle house. Four roads come down to it out of the hills. Cattle are driven over at the ebb with a great deal of shouting, and it smells of dung, turf smoke and the river.
sites.source: Áth Cliath, the ford of hurdles, where the Slige Midluachra crosses: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Dublin_to_795. A ferryman is the dossier's inference; none is named

sites.name: The church in the ring
sites.see: A wooden church with a steep shingled roof inside a wide pear-shaped bank, with a few round cells, a stone cross slab and a graveyard of small plain markers all facing east. A hand-bell stands on the sill. The light comes in at the west door and falls on an altar with one good cloth. It is very quiet: there are more cells than monks.
sites.source: The enclosure of about five hectares: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Dublin_to_795. Whether the house was still alive in 793 is doubtful (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Scandinavian_Dublin): the game makes it half empty and names no abbot

sites.name: The guest-house at the gate
sites.see: A round house of woven hazel just inside the gap in the bank, its door never barred, a fire in the middle and a bench round the wall. Goods are laid out on a hide before the door, and three or four men stand by as sureties while a bargain is said aloud. There is a tub of water for a guest's feet, and it smells of oat bread and wet wool.
sites.source: A stranger trades only under a protector, with sureties, for a gift and first choice: Design/content/realms/irish_sea.md; peoples/irish_gaelic.md (after F. Kelly, not quoted). No market is recorded here before 841: this is a guest's bargain, not a market

sites.name: Máel Ruain's house at Tallaght
sites.see: A morning's walk south-west toward the hills: a tight bank, a small church, and cells in rows, everything swept. Monks in undyed wool stand in a stream to the knees saying psalms. In the writing hut a man rules lines on calfskin by the light of the door. No ale is brewed here and it can be smelt that none is.
sites.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%A1el_Ruain; E. J. Gwynn and W. J. Purton, The Monastery of Tallaght (1911), sections 6 and following, via peoples/irish_gaelic.md. The psalms in cold water are the custom of the clients of God (?)

sites.name: The ship-fort
sites.see: A raw turf bank with a fence of split oak on top, open to the river, and inside it a row of long hulls drawn up on rollers with their masts down. Tents and booths of sailcloth stand between the ships; a larger house with a carved door is the king's from 853. Armed men sit mending gear. It smells of tar, wood smoke and too many people.
sites.source: Annals of Ulster 841; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Scandinavian_Dublin. No trace of the fort has been dug and its place is not known: the picture is the game's. The king's share on the strand is not recorded (?)

sites.name: The strand of the captives
sites.see: A stretch of hard sand below the bank where people sit roped by the ankle in rows, sorted by tongue, with a dealer's man walking between them and a folding scale laid on a sea chest. Buyers look at teeth and hands. Behind them hides are stacked as high as a man. Nobody shouts. After 980 the rows are Britons, English and Welsh, and no Irish.
sites.source: Captives and church silver out, grain and wine in: Design/content/realms/irish_sea.md; economy/furs_amber_ivory_slaves.md. Folding scales and weights lay in the graves up the river: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilmainham. That no Irish slave was held after 980 is the annalist's boast

sites.name: The grave field by the weir
sites.see: Up the river where the tide ends, low mounds in the gravel beside an old Irish church, each with a post or a stone and some with a spear standing in them. Young men lie here with a sword, a shield and a comb; women with two oval brooches; a smith with his tongs. Wind in the grass, and the weir talking below.
sites.source: Kilmainham and Islandbridge, the largest grave field of the Northmen in the west outside their own lands: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilmainham; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Scandinavian_Dublin

sites.name: The landing at the long stone
sites.see: A tall grey standing stone on the strand east of the town, and below it a bank of clay and wattle where hulls lie side by side at high water and dry on the ebb. Porters carry casks up a plank path to a gate in an earth bank. The king's man sits on an upturned boat with a scale. Tar, fish, and the smoke of two hundred hearths.
sites.source: The Long Stone at the landing stood into the 17th century (dossier, from memory (?)); the bank of about 950: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wood_Quay. The king's man on the strand: Design/content/realms/irish_sea.md (the amount is not recorded)

sites.name: The plank street
sites.see: A lane of split logs laid over mud, running down to the river between wattle fences, and behind each fence a low thatched house with its door to the path. Combs, shoes, amber beads and turned bowls are sold from the doorways; antler chips and leather offcuts lie ankle deep. Children sail toy boats in the gutter. It smells of tanning, smoke and pigs.
sites.source: Wood Quay and Fishamble Street, dug 1973 to 1981: fourteen fenced plots rebuilt on the same lines; comb-makers, amber and jet workers, shoemakers, turners; toy boats (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wood_Quay; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Scandinavian_Dublin)

sites.name: The king's hall
sites.see: The largest house in the town, on the height above the pool: a long wattle hall with four great roof posts, a fire down the middle and benches both sides. Shields hang on the wall and a poet stands by the king's seat. Men speak Norse at one end and Irish at the other. Meat smoke, ale, wet dogs, and silk on the high bench.
sites.source: The kings of the Foreigners: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Dublin. The hall itself has not been found; houses with four roof posts and side benches are those of Fishamble Street. A poet of each tongue: Cináed ua hArtacáin praised Amlaíb Cuarán (?)

sites.name: The yard on the strand
sites.see: A long keel on blocks above the tide line with half her strakes on, pale oak against the mud, and men splitting a log with wedges beside her. Steam rises from a plank being bent over a fire. Rivets in a bucket, a tar pot, a boy with a hair rope. The noise is axes and one man counting.
sites.source: Skuldelev 2, thirty metres and sixty oars, built in the Dublin area about 1042 of Irish oak: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skuldelev_ships. Shipwrights among the crafts of the town (?)

sites.name: The ale-house by the ford road
sites.see: A wattle house larger than its neighbours, just inside the west gate where the road from the ford comes in, with a bush tied over the door. Inside: one hearth, two benches, a vat, a board for dice, and men of three tongues who have stopped noticing it. A woman with keys at her belt knows every one of them. Malt, smoke and boiled mutton.
sites.source: invented; the house is of the Fishamble Street kind (a central hearth and two side benches: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Scandinavian_Dublin). Ale-wives are named in the law of Chester, this town's partner (dossier legacaestir)

sites.name: The law mound
sites.see: A steep green mound as high as six men, south of the river and outside the bank, with a flat top and a ring of posts. On a law day the free men of the town stand round its foot and the speakers on its side, and a case is said aloud twice so that none can claim not to have heard. Wind, and gulls from the strand.
sites.source: The Thingmote, forty feet high and two hundred and forty round, levelled in 1685: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Dublin. It is written of only later, so its use in these years is not certain (?)

sites.name: The moneyer's house
sites.see: A plot like any other, but with a barred door and a man at it. Inside, a block with a die set in it, a hammer, shears, and a pan of blanks; the moneyer lays a blank, strikes once, and drops a penny with the king's head on it into a bowl. Each coin is weighed. The sound carries down the street like a slow smith.
sites.source: Pennies from about 995 to 997, copies of Æthelred's, with Sitriuc's name and the town's: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Dublin; chronicle_793.json 997-dublin-coins. No mint building is known. The moneyer's name Færemin is on the coins (?)

sites.name: Holy Trinity on the height
sites.see: A new church of oak staves and shingles on the highest ground in the town, above the river plots, with a wooden cross on the gable and the chips of its building still in the mud. A bishop with an English way of singing says Mass. From the door the whole bay can be seen, and the ships on the strand below.
sites.source: Founded probably soon after 1028 by King Sitriuc, with Dúnán as first bishop; of wood; endowed with Baldoyle, Raheny and Portrane: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christ_Church_Cathedral,_Dublin. The game opens it in 1030

people.name: Tipraite
people.looks: Near sixty, spare and upright, grey hair to the collar, a brown wool cloak over a long linen shirt, a bronze ring-pin at the shoulder, a bundle of notched tally sticks in his hand.
people.trait: Keeper of the church's land and its guest-house since the last abbot died: careful, hospitable by law and by nature, and tired of being asked when there will be an abbot again.
people.want: Wine for the Mass, salt before the slaughter, and a guest whose word holds, so that the kin who own this church remember it is worth keeping.
people.fear: That the king of Tara's men cross the river again and find a church with no abbot to shame them; and, after the year Rechru burned, any sail he cannot name.
people.voice: Slow and exact. Says what a thing costs in cows, names the sureties before the goods, and begins an answer with 'Not hard to tell.'
knows: how a stranger gets a protector, and what a bargain without sureties is worth: nothing
worth in cows, séts and ounces, and what wine, salt and iron fetch at this gate
who is king in Leinster and who across the river in Brega, and which of them is burning what
the days of the fairs at Tailtiu and Carman, and whether they will be held
which houses of the saints are a morning's walk from here, and who is strict in them

ties.note: His sister's son. The ferryman sends strangers to the gate, and the steward sends them back to be piloted out.
Walks to Tallaght for the feast of Máel Ruain and comes back hungry. Lends the writing hut his best calfskins.
From 807 he lodges Columba's people when they land for Kells, and finds them carts (invented).
The same man, at his own house on the island.
The old abbot of Hī once sent this church a bell-shrine's worth of wax in a bad year (invented).

lines.greet: A boat from over the sea, and no host. Sit, wash your feet. Until I say you are my guest you are a grey dog here, and anyone may kick you.
lines.greet_again: My guest again. Good. The sureties are the same three men, and one of them has been asking after your wine since the cattle went up.
rumour: There has been no abbot since Siadal. The kin argue over whose son it should be. Meanwhile I count the calves, and God, I hope, counts me.
The king of Leinster was burned in a house with his queen. The man who lit it is king now. I have sent him a cask, as I sent the last.
The fishermen saw smoke off Rechru for three days. They say the ships had no oars showing and went like gulls. I have buried the altar cup.
Tallaght stopped the king's fair once, so that not a horse ran. A strict house can do what an army cannot. Remember it when you deal with them.
lines.saying: Three sureties, three witnesses, and then the goods. A bargain said to the wind is the wind's.
lines.farewell: Go with the ebb, and take my sister's son over the bar. If you come back, come to this gate first. It does not close.

people.source: invented; the name is in the Annals of Ulster (names_placeholder.json). No abbot is named after Siadal (dossier, section 1), so he is a lay keeper, not an abbot. The stranger as a grey dog, sureties, and the open guest-house: peoples/irish_gaelic.md (after Kelly; Meyer 1911 for the open door).

people.name: Óengus
people.looks: About forty-five in 793, lean, the tonsure grown grey at the edges, a patched undyed habit with the hood back, ink on two fingers, a wax tablet tied to his belt with a thong.
people.trait: Máel Ruain's pupil, a client of God at Tallaght, making a calendar in verse with a saint for every day of the year: exact, dry, and kinder than his rule.
people.want: The names and days of saints kept in churches over the sea, good calfskin, and ink that does not fade; and nobody to make a fuss of him.
people.fear: To die with days of the year still empty; and monks who wander abroad and call it pilgrimage, which his master forbade.
people.voice: Short, learned, amused. Counts on his fingers while he talks. Never raises his voice and never drinks your ale.
knows: the feast of every saint he has heard of, and which churches keep them
what a book costs in calves and in a scribe's year, and who would pay it
the rule of Tallaght: no ale, no meat but deer and wild pig, no wandering
Latin, and how to read a merchant's letter for him without smiling
which abbots are lords with spears, and which are afraid of them

ties.note: The steward brings skins and gossip; Óengus pays in prayers and corrections.
Wants to see what Columba's people are carrying to Kells, and will ask politely once (invented).
Has Hī's list of its own saints by letter and wants its dates checked.
Never met. He wants Willibrord's day from the Frisians' own church, since Willibrord studied in Ireland twelve years (?).
By letter only: Lindisfarne is Columba's daughter house, and its dead are prayed for here.
the ferryman carries his letters over the river, and brings him every stranger's news, uninvited
the abbot of Hi after Cellach, a client of God like himself: they send each other feast days

lines.greet: A merchant. Good. Tell me what saint your church at home keeps, and on what day. No, I want nothing else. Sit, you are standing in my light.
lines.greet_again: You again, and I have filled eleven days since. Have you a name for me from over the water, or only casks?
rumour: My master said the ale that makes men forget God would not be drunk here. So we remember God, and are thirsty.
A brother asked leave to go abroad as a pilgrim. He was told the hardest road is the one to the church door each night.
I have a day in harvest with no saint in it. If a holy man died among the Frisians about then, I would count it a kindness.
New skin, bad ink. I say nothing more. If you carry oak galls from the Franks, I will find something to give you.
lines.saying: To go to Rome is much trouble and little profit. The king you look for there you will not find unless you bring him.
lines.farewell: Go safely. If you pass a church, ask whose day they keep and when. I will know if you guess.

people.source: Real: Óengus son of Óengoba, the Culdee, pupil of Máel Ruain at Tallaght, who wrote a calendar of the saints in verse about 800 (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%A1el_Ruain; the dates of his birth and death are guesses (?)). That he questioned a merchant for saints' days is invented. The ale: The Monastery of Tallaght 6 (Gwynn and Purton 1911), retold. The saying: 'To go to Rome', Kuno Meyer, Selections from Ancient Irish Poetry (1911), retold in prose. The ink: scribes' margins, Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus II (1903).

people.name: Suibne
people.looks: Thirty-three in 793, short and wide, black hair tied back, bare legs brown to the knee, a rough grey cloak with a thorn for a pin, a long sounding pole worn pale by his hands.
people.trait: Ferryman at the hurdles and the only man who knows where the bar lies this year: cheerful, nosy, and keeps a tally in his head of every boat that has come in.
people.want: A boat of planks like yours, one day; and meanwhile the first look at whatever comes up the river, and a share in the telling of it.
people.fear: A fleet in the bay on a flood tide, with his children on the strand. He counts sails before he counts anything else.
people.voice: Quick, plain, a talker. Says distances by tides and names the wind by what it does to the smoke.
knows: the bar and the channels of the bay, and how they moved last winter
when the hurdles are dry and how deep the pool is at each tide
who crossed the ford this month, with how many cattle, going which way
every boat that has lain in the pool in his time, and its master's face
where the four roads go, and which king's land each one is in

ties.note: His mother's brother. Suibne brings him strangers and is paid in bread.
Carries the monk's letters over the river and thinks him the cleverest man alive.
Pilots Columba's boats over the bar from 807, and will take no fee from the saint's people.
The same man.
Asked the Northman where he was from, twice, and got two answers. Watches him.

lines.greet: I saw you off the head at first light. You came in a spear's length from the bar and never knew. Next time wave, and I will come out.
lines.greet_again: The same boat, a little lower in the water. Trade is good, then. The bar has moved a ship's length south since you left; follow me in.
rumour: Forty head of cattle crossed yesterday going north, and no herdsman I knew. Somebody is paying a fine, or stealing one.
A boat of hide went out with three monks and no steering oar. I asked where to. They said God knew. I hope he told them.
They took women off Benn Étair, a whole strand of them. My wife will not go down for weed now unless I stand on the rock.
Sixty sails on this river, and sixty more on the Boyne. I counted till the tide turned. I did not wave.
lines.saying: The river tells you its depth twice a day. A man who drowns here was not listening.
lines.farewell: Out on the ebb, keep the head on your left hand and the smoke behind you. I will have your tally when you come back.

people.source: invented; the name is in the Annals of Ulster. The ford of hurdles and the shifting bar: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Dublin_to_795; Research/water_levels/ireland_isles.md. The pilgrims' boat without oars is the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle's of 891, told here early as a thing such men did. Howth 821 and the sixty ships of 837: dossier, section 5; he speaks of each only after its year.

people.name: Vemundr
people.looks: About forty, heavy in the shoulder, fair beard in two plaits, a blue wool cloak with a silver ring-pin of Irish work, a folding bronze scale in a leather case on his belt.
people.trait: Dealer in captives on the strand below the fort: sober, fair by his own measure, remembers every lot and every buyer, and has an Irish wife who reckons faster than he does.
people.want: Grain, wine and salt for the winter, a buyer who comes back, and a son who can speak to an Irish king without a go-between.
people.fear: A bad winter in the fort with too many mouths roped on his strand; and the day the kings fall out, which he has seen once.
people.voice: Says little and less than he means. Names a weight once. Calls a great loss 'not the best day'.
knows: what a captive of each people fetches here, at York and in the east, by weight of silver
which king's ships are out, where, and when they are looked for home
the northern ounce, the nick test, and who on this strand has a light scale
what the fort lacks this month: it is always grain
which Irish kings sell to him and which only shout

ties.note: Learned the trade as a boy at the Schlei from the house of Asulf, the dealer who remembered every lot (invented).
Still sends that house a share of amber's worth each third summer.
The English of York buy their own kin back through that family's heirs, and beat him down on price.
Rorik's man at Dorestad buys Irish cloaks and asks no questions about the hands that wove them.
the reeve of the English kings' rock, whose brother's son sat in his rows after the rock on the Clyde fell; an uncle slow to pay

lines.greet: A Frisian keel. You have a scale, I hope. Mine is true, but you should not have to take a stranger's word for his own weights.
lines.greet_again: You came back. Most do not, after the first look at my strand. Sit. I have grain to buy before I have anything to sell.
rumour: The kings went north to the rock on the Clyde. Four months, they say. When they come home there will be more people than hides.
An Irish king sold me forty of his neighbour's herdsmen. Next summer the neighbour sold me thirty of his. I asked for neither.
Ímar is dead. It was quick and it was not a wound. Men here do not say more, and I would not ask.
The other Foreigners came in with the tide and wrecked the bank. Not the best day. I was trading again by the new moon.
lines.saying: A man is worth what he can do with his hands. A lord is worth what his kin will weigh out. Ask which you have before you feed him.
lines.farewell: Fair wind. Bring rye, bring wine. And if you buy from me, do not sell south to the Franks: they ask where a Christian came from.

people.source: invented; the name from names_placeholder.json (Vé- + -mundr). Captives out and grain wanted, 841 to 902: Design/content/realms/irish_sea.md. The fleet of 871 and Ímar's death in 873: dossier, section 5. Scales in the graves at Kilmainham: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilmainham. Christians not to be sold to the Franks: spine, thread holy_island. He speaks of each event only after its year.

people.name: Arnfinnr
people.looks: Thirty in 917, tall and stooped, red-brown hair going thin, a green tunic with a silk band at the neck, one silver arm-ring given by a king, a rune-cut stick behind his belt.
people.trait: The king's poet in the new hall: born in the old fort, carried out of it as a boy in 902, and come back with the fleet. Proud, exact about words, and bitter in a quiet way.
people.want: Somebody who can answer him. And, more than he says, to know what became of the silver his father's fellows put in the ground when they fled.
people.fear: That the old questions die on the benches because the young men would rather hear about pennies.
people.voice: Measured, a little grand, then suddenly plain. Asks before he tells. Understates everything but the gods.
knows: the questions Odin put to the wise giant, in their order, and who holds the next one
who of the fort's people went to Man, the Wirral and the Ribble in 902
the kings of his house at York and here, and which is in favour this season
what a king will give for a good verse and for a bad one
that the men who taught him sat on a bench with men who knew an old Northman called Ravn

ties.note: At two removes: his teacher's teacher shared a bench with Ravn. He has one riddle he says came down from him.
The poet of the kings at York holds the next question of the giant's line and thinks York the better hall.
His mother's kin followed Hingamund to the Wirral in 902 and stayed there.
In his last years he drinks in her mother's ale-house and tells the child the giants' names.
A Norse-born brother on Hī, once of this hall, who still knows the last question (invented).
the grandson of Ímar who brought the fleet back in 917: his first king, and the one he measures the rest by

lines.greet: A merchant in the king's hall. You have a face that has been asked things. Sit below the fire. Do you buy words, or only hides?
lines.greet_again: The man who answers. I have kept a seat and a question. The second is easier to keep than the first, in this hall.
rumour: I was nine when the Irish came over the bank. We left ships half built. My father carried a chest, and then one day he was not carrying it.
The king's kin hold York again this year. Next year, who knows. A poet learns two sets of praise and keeps both dry.
Our ships came home from England a few at a time. Five kings dead, they say. I have verses for three of them and no hall quiet enough.
There is a river in the English land, south bank, where the Wirral men will not dig. Ask them why. They will tell you a different river.
lines.saying: The earth was made of a giant's flesh and the sea of his blood. So do not complain to me that the crossing was rough.
lines.farewell: Go well. When you know who the eldest of that kin was, come back and say it to my face, not to York's.

people.source: invented; the name from names_placeholder.json (Arn- + -finnr). The riddles are those of the lay of Vafthruthnir (Bellows 1923; riddles_793.json set ymirs_kin, sold here from 917). The flight of 902 and the return of 917: dossier, section 5; Brunanburh 937: chronicle_793.json. That the silver found at Cuerdale by the Ribble was buried by the men of 902 is a common reading, not a fact (?).

people.name: Affraic
people.looks: Forty-two in 980, broad and quick, dark hair under a linen cap, a red-brown wool gown pinned with one oval brooch that was her father's mother's, keys and a small knife at her belt.
people.trait: Keeper of the ale-house by the ford road: an Irish mother, a Norse father, both tongues and neither side's patience. Descended, she says, from the ferrymen of the hurdles.
people.want: Custom from both ends of the hall, malt at a fair price, and her daughter married to a man with a plot and no ship.
people.fear: A siege. She was a girl when the town burned, and she has kept a full water butt ever since.
people.voice: Fast, dry, switches tongue in the middle of a sentence. Remembers what you drank and what you owed.
knows: who is in the town, who has left, and who is hiring hands for which ship
the price of malt, hides and a plot on the plank street, this season and last
what the king's man takes on the strand, and when he can be talked to
which Irish king is over the town this year, and what he wants at Christmas
the old tale of the ford: a boat a spear's length from the bar, and a ferryman who waved

ties.note: Six or seven generations down, by her own count. The house's boat is in the family's stories.
The young king drank here before he was king and has never been allowed to forget his tally.
The old poet taught her the giants' names when she was a child, and she can still say the first question.
Buys Droitwich salt through a woman who brews by the Dee, and sends her news of whose ship is coming.
The abbot of Hī buried the old king. She sends the island a cask each Columba's feast for it.
the old king's men drank in her house; she holds a tally stick of his, unpaid, and would not take payment for it now

lines.greet: Shut the door, you are letting the smoke out. Frisian? My people have a story about a Frisian boat. Sit down and I will see if it is you.
lines.greet_again: There he is. You owe me for two cups from last time, and I owe you a story. We will call it even if you bring salt.
rumour: The king of Tara stood at the gate and every Irish slave in the town walked out past him. I lost a cook. I did not mind as much as I said.
Old Amlaíb asked for a boat to Columba's island. A king all his life, and he went out like a pilgrim with one bag.
An ounce of gold on every plot, each Christmas night. I asked the steward if he took ale instead. He did not laugh. He drank it, though.
The year they shut us in we drank the sea. I boiled it with barley and called it broth. Nobody asked for a second bowl.
lines.saying: Three things a house cannot hide: smoke, a full vat, and a man who owes.
lines.farewell: Mind the bar, it has moved. My people always say that. One year it will be true and you will thank me.

people.source: invented; the name is in the Annals of Ulster (peoples/irish_gaelic.md, women's names). Tara and the freeing of the slaves, 980; the siege with only sea water and the Christmas gold, 989: Annals of Tigernach, via Design/content/realms/irish_sea.md. The descent from the ferryman is the game's thread across the centuries. The saying is invented in the manner of the Triads. She speaks of each event only after its year.

people.name: Sitriuc
people.looks: About thirty in 1000, slight, a fine fair beard combed and oiled, a red silk cap and a cloak edged with marten, a short sword in a gilt scabbard, a new penny turned over and over in his fingers.
people.trait: King of the Foreigners of Dyflin for forty years: Amlaíb Cuarán's son by an Irish queen, husband of Brian's daughter, a man who loses battles and keeps the town.
people.want: Coin with his name that men will take across the sea, a bishop of his own, and to be on the winning side by evening without having left the wall.
people.fear: His Irish in-laws, all of them; a second siege with no water; and a son in another king's hands.
people.voice: Smooth, quick, at home in two tongues and a little Latin. Jokes at his own cost. Changes the subject to trade when war is mentioned.
knows: what his pennies weigh, whose they copy, and where they are taken at face
every king on both sides of the sea and whose daughter each one married
what the town owes the king of Tara each Christmas, to the ounce
who is building ships, for whom, and who will pay for them
the road to Rome, after 1028, and what it cost him

ties.note: His later pennies copy Cnut's, and Dyflin's ships sail in that king's peace; they were allies against the Welsh about 1030 (?).
A tally of ale from his youth, which she will not let him pay, since a king in debt is a king who listens.
Took the wright's father into the town and gave the son his first keel to lay.
The king's reeve at the Dee takes the first sight of Dyflin's marten skins and four pence a load. Sitriuc thinks it too much.
His father died a penitent on Hī under Abbot Mugrón. He sends the island gifts and does not go.
his father, who gave up the kingship after Tara and died a penitent on Hi
the rich man of York whose ships carry Dyflin's pennies over the hills, and bring York's news back (?)
a skipper of the islands who pays the king's man on the strand without argument, and carries Dyflin's pennies north
a moneyer on the Dee who sold him a bag of new English pennies and the pattern of a worn die

lines.greet: A Frisian house. Old, I am told. Look at this and say what you see. A penny, yes. Now read me whose. Good. Sit by me.
lines.greet_again: My Frisian. Tell me truthfully, as you would not tell my moneyer: do they take my pennies at Chester, or weigh them?
rumour: My father wore one sandal's worth of a nickname all his life. They call me for my beard. A king here is known by what a woman might notice.
I watched the battle from the wall with my wife. She said her father's men were winning. I said the tide was. We were both right.
I have been to Rome. It is far, and every bishop on the road keeps a toll. I came home wanting one of my own.
They hold my son for twelve hundred cows and six score Welsh horses. Cows I have. Do you know a man in Anglesey with a deep boat?
lines.saying: A town is a ship that cannot sail away. So you learn to make friends with the weather.
lines.farewell: Go in my peace as far as it reaches, which is the bar. After that, be quick.

people.source: Real: Sitriuc Silkbeard, king of Dublin 989 or 995 to 1036, died 1042; son of Amlaíb Cuarán and Gormflaith, husband of Brian's daughter Sláine; struck the first pennies about 995 to 997; stayed inside at Clontarf in 1014; went to Rome in 1028; founded Holy Trinity; his son's ransom in 1029 (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigtrygg_Silkbeard; dossier). His birth year is a guess (?). That he watched from the wall with his wife is from the 12th-century tale, not the annals. Every line and every dealing with a merchant is the game's. He speaks of each event only after its year.

people.name: Asgrimr
people.looks: Forty in 1042, thick-armed, a short grey-fair beard full of chips, a leather apron over a russet tunic, a small wooden cross on a thong, a broad axe he never puts down.
people.trait: Master of the yard on the strand, and the man who lays the keel of the sixty-oar ship: slow to promise, quicker to build, and unable to pass a hull without knocking on it.
people.want: Straight oak from the Leinster woods before somebody burns them, iron for ten thousand rivets, and one ship of his that people will talk about.
people.fear: Green timber, a king who changes before the ship is paid for, and fire in the yard.
people.voice: Slow, flat, technical. Talks of ships as 'she' and of kings as weather. Never says a ship is good; says 'she will do'.
knows: every hull on the strand, her age, her wright and what is wrong with her
what a ship costs by the oar, and how long from keel to sail
where the oak comes from and which Irish king must be paid for it
who is hiring crews this winter and for whose war
how a small Danish boat like your house's first one was put together, and what he would change

ties.note: The old king gave him his first keel. He builds for whoever is king after, and says so.
Chester buys Dyflin ships and then fines their skippers forty shillings for coming up the Dee without leave.
A wright on the Ouse who trades him iron for seasoned knees, by letter of mouth through skippers.
As a young man he mended two of that king's ships on this strand and was paid in good English pennies (invented).
an island skipper with a boat building in the yard, half paid for: a patient man, for a Northman

lines.greet: That boat. Danish-built, small, old in her lines. Who keeps a thing like that sailing? Bring her up on the rollers and let me look underneath.
lines.greet_again: She is still afloat, then. I told the boy she would be. I have a strake of dry oak put by with your house's mark on it.
rumour: I have a keel laid thirty paces long. Sixty oars. The king who ordered her may not be the king who launches her. She will not care.
An English earl's son is in the town hiring crews. He pays in pennies of the right weight. I have never seen men so keen to row.
The Leinster king has the town now. He came to the yard first, before the hall. A man who knows what he has taken.
The oak comes dearer each year. Somebody burned a wood to spite somebody's god. A wood does not grow back for a grandson.
lines.saying: A ship is a hundred small things that must all be done. A king is one large thing that need not be.
lines.farewell: Keep her tarred, and off the sand when it blows from the east. If you sink her, come back anyway. I build.

people.source: invented; the name from names_placeholder.json (Ás- + -grímr). The ship: Skuldelev 2, built in the Dublin area about 1042 of Irish oak, thirty metres and sixty oars (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skuldelev_ships). Harold Godwinson wintering 1051 to 1052 and Diarmait taking the town in 1052: Design/content/realms/irish_sea.md. Tomar's wood burned in 1000: lore/gods_cult.md. Forty shillings a man for coming up the Dee without leave: Domesday Book for Chester, via realms/irish_sea.md. He speaks of each event only after its year.

people.name: Amlaíb Cuarán
people.trait: King of the foreigners of Dublin for most of forty years, and twice king at York before the English put him out: shrewd, amused, baptised with a king for godfather. In 980, after his sons lose at Tara, an old man who gives it all up and goes to Colum Cille's island a penitent, and finds he is curious about his own soul.
people.want: To die on the saint's island and lie in its ground; and, against his own resolve, to hear what is happening in Dublin.
people.fear: That penance, like everything else he did, has come a little too late to be believed.
people.voice: Slow, amused, a king's habit of expecting an answer. Norse and Irish in the same sentence.
people.looks: Past fifty and looking seventy, big-framed and gone gaunt, white beard cut short, a penitent's coarse grey tunic with the mark of arm-rings still pale on his wrists, one plain sandal mended with cord.
people.note: One man under one id. From 945 to 980 he is met in the king's hall at Dublin (the plain lines). In 980 and 981 he is met as a penitent in the guest house on Hi (hi.guest_house): the lines that begin penitent_ are his there, and want, fear, voice and looks are those of his last year.
knows: the price of everything that was ever sold on the Liffey strand, slaves above all
York from the inside: its archbishops, its moneyers and how its kings are put out
every sea-lord between Man and Orkney by his father and his debts
what was agreed at the gate of Dublin after Tara, and what it cost

ties.note: his son by Gormlaith of Leinster, who will be king in Dublin and strike its first pennies
the alewife by the Liffey whose house his men drank in; she still holds a tally stick of his, unpaid
a York reeve who remembers him as king there and is careful not to say so (?)
the king's reeve on the Dee, who fines his skippers each summer and dines him each winter
the abbot who receives him on Hi as a penitent in 980, and sees him into Oran's ground

lines.greet: A Frisian in my hall. Sit below the salt, wherever that is today; my steward keeps moving it. What do you carry, and what will you swear it is worth?
lines.greet_again: The Frisian again. I have been king in York since you were last here, and am not now. Do not ask. Drink.
rumour: I was baptised in England with a king for godfather. He gave me gifts. Three winters later his people handed me my cloak. I kept the gifts.
They call me the sandal. A king here is named for what a child might notice. My father was named for worse.
The reeve on the Dee fines my skippers every summer and dines with me every winter. We understand each other. It costs me forty shillings a ship.
lines.saying: A town is held by the king its merchants would miss least. I try to be missed a little.
lines.farewell: Go in my peace, as far as the bar. Pay my man on the strand. He is honest, which I allow in one man at a time.
lines.penitent_greet: I had a hall once with a door wide enough for six men abreast. Here I duck my head. Sit, merchant. Do you come from the Liffey?
lines.penitent_greet_again: You again. Good. The monks will not tell me what a slave fetches in Dublin now. Tell me, and then tell me to repent of asking.
penitent_rumour: At Tara my sons lost in a day what took me forty years. Then the king of Tara stood at my gate and every Irish slave walked out free.
I was king in York twice and they put me out twice. The English are polite about it. They hand you your cloak.
I was baptised in England with a king for godfather, and meant about half of it. I am here to make up the other half.
lines.penitent_saying: A sandal fits one foot at a time. Mine is on my son's now.
lines.penitent_farewell: If you go to Dublin, tell Sitriuc his father sleeps on straw and sleeps well. He will not believe either part.

people.source: Annals of Tigernach 980 (Design/content/realms/irish_sea.json; chronicle_793.json 980-tara); en.wikipedia Amlaib Cuaran: king at York about 941-944 and 949-952, baptised 943 with King Edmund as sponsor (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 943), died on Hi in 980 or 981. He was not at Tara himself. 'Cuaran' means sandal. His birth year is a guess (?). The lines are the game's. One person in the weave of 7 Oct 2026: this row was hi.amlaib in hi.json and is the 'duiblinn.amlaib_cuaran' of legacaestir.json's ties. He is placed at Dublin, where he was king from 945 to 947 and from 952 to 980, and is met on Hi only in his last year. The Dublin lines are invented.

people.name: Cerball
people.trait: King of Leinster, who with the king of Brega drove the foreigners out of the fort and left their ships half built on the strand: vigorous, proud, a friend to poets, and not sure what to do with an empty harbour.
people.want: Wine and salt landed at the pool as they were before the foreigners came, under his own protection and for his own gifts.
people.fear: The grandsons of Ímar coming back with a fleet; and a horse that shies.
people.voice: Loud, generous, fond of his own stories; speaks to a merchant as to a guest, and to a guest as to a witness.
people.looks: About forty, big, red-bearded, a many-coloured cloak with a gold brooch the width of a hand, a sword with an ivory hilt that he likes to be asked about, poets and hounds at his heels.
knows: how the fort was taken, who fled where, and how many ships were left on the strand
the kings of Leinster, Brega and Tara, and which of them he trusts this season
what a king's protection is worth to a stranger, and what gift earns it
that the foreigners' sword he carries was taken in the fort, and whose it was

ties.note: drove him out of the fort in 902; hears that he sits on English sand now and looks at English walls

lines.greet: A ship in the pool, and not a foreigner's! Come up, merchant. Half a year ago you would have paid a pirate for this mooring. Now you pay nobody. Remember who arranged that.
lines.greet_again: My Frisian. Sit by me. Tell the company what the foreigners' fort looks like now, with my cattle in it.
rumour: We drove them out half dead, and they left a good number of their ships behind. I walk down sometimes to look at the keels. Fine work. A pity about the owners.
They say the old chief of the fort went begging to a king of the Britons, and then to an English lady, who gave him sand. I hope he likes sand.
A harbour with no ships in it is a field with no cows. I am told that merchants can be grown, like barley, if a king is patient. I am trying to be patient.
lines.saying: A fort is easy to take and hard to fill.
lines.farewell: Go under my protection as far as the bar. Tell them over the water that the pool is open, and the king generous.

people.source: Cerball son of Muirecán, king of Leinster, died 909 (Annals of Ulster 909 (?)); with Máel Finnia of Brega he drove the foreigners from the fort at Áth Cliath in 902, and they left a great number of their ships (Annals of Ulster 902; chronicle_793.json 902-dublin-expelled). Made real in the weave of 7 Oct 2026 to answer legacaestir.json's tie from Hingamund. His birth year is a guess; that a merchant met him at the empty pool, his looks and his words are invented.

people.name: Sitriuc Cáech
people.trait: Grandson of Ímar, called the One-eyed: took the pool back with a fleet in 917, killed a king of Tara outside it, and already has his good eye on York.
people.want: Silver, ships and men enough to hold Dublin and take York; a town at his back that pays.
people.fear: His own kinsmen with fleets; and being remembered as the lesser grandson.
people.voice: Brief and hard, with a soldier's jokes; talks of towns as of ships to be manned.
people.looks: Forty, rangy, a scarred lid over one blind eye, a grey-fair beard cut square, a red cloak over mail that he does not take off in town, a heavy silver arm ring on each wrist.
knows: how the pool was retaken, and what the Irish kings paid or lost for it
what York's hall holds, and who of his kin sits in it this year
what cut silver, captives and hides fetch between the Liffey and the Ribble
which plots in the new town are his to give

ties.note: the Chester moneyer strikes plain pennies that his men will take only by weight; he calls them thin, and takes them
the York poet has a praise-poem ready for him; he has heard the first half, and will pay when he hears the rest in York
his hall's poet, who was a boy in the old fort and never lets him forget whose it was

lines.greet: A trader. Good. A town is a ship that wants a crew, and I am short of every trade but fighting. Lie where you like. Pay my man. Come back.
lines.greet_again: The Frisian. You came back to a town three winters old. Either you are a fool or you can count. I am hoping you can count.
rumour: My grandfather held this pool, and the Irish threw my uncles out of it. I have put that right. Now I am told there is a hall at York with my kin's name on the door.
The king of Tara came to take the town back, with twelve kings behind him. He is under the turf at the ford now. The twelve went home.
A moneyer on the Dee strikes pennies with no king on them. My men will not take them by tale. By weight they take anything.
lines.saying: A man with one eye looks twice at everything. It has kept me alive.
lines.farewell: Go, and tell them on the Dee that the pool has a king in it again.

people.source: Sitriuc grandson of Ímar, called Cáech ('one-eyed' or 'squinting'): retook Dublin in 917, defeated and killed Niall Glúndub, king of Tara, outside it in 919, left for York in 920, was king there from 921, married a sister of King Æthelstan in 926 and died in 927 (Annals of Ulster 917, 919, 920, 927; Anglo-Saxon Chronicle D 925-926 (?); chronicle_793.json 917-dublin-retaken). Made real in the weave of 7 Oct 2026 to answer legacaestir.json's tie from the moneyer Irfara. His birth year, looks and words are invented.

stories.title: A chest for Kells
stories.summary: After the killing on Hī in 806 Abbot Cellach builds a new house for Columba inland in Ireland, and the things of the island must cross the sea in somebody's hull. The pool is where they land, and the merchant is asked to carry a chest whose contents nobody names.
stories.picture: Monks in grey wool wading ashore at a dark pool at dawn, two of them carrying a long chest wrapped in oiled hide on poles, a brisk abbot with rolled sleeves pointing inland, a Frisian boat behind them on the mud.

beats.text: Cellach counts hands and boats. He asks whether a planked hull would carry timber, lead and one chest to the black pool, and says the chest goes under the merchant's own bench.
The chest is landed at the pool. Suibne brings the boat over the bar and will take no fee from Columba's people. Cellach is already asking the price of carts.
Tipraite stands surety for the merchant on the road north-west and finds oxen. He asks no question about the chest, and looks at it a long time.

beats.when: year >= 807 and year < 815 and not flag.duiblinn_chest_opened
beats.text: Óengus asks, once, to see inside. The monk with the key looks at the merchant. Inside are gatherings of a great gospel book, some pages painted and some bare.
A man of the king of Brega waits across the ford. He says his lord would give ten cows for one painted leaf, to lay on a sick child. Nobody need know.
Word has gone back to the island before the boat. The brothers who stayed ask the merchant what the new church looks like, and whether it has a wall.

endings.how: The merchant carried the chest whole to the carts and saw it on the road to Kells.
endings.text: The house of Columba writes the merchant's name where it writes its friends'. Every church of that family, from Hī to Kells, gives him a host.
endings.reward: flag bk_carried; deed carried_letters; a protector at every house of Columba's family, so he may trade there without a gift; Cellach friendly, and Óengus's prayers; about 240 d in wax and fine cloaks

endings.how: He let the king of Brega's man have one painted leaf.
endings.text: Ten cows change hands at the ford. Nobody speaks of it. Cellach counts the gatherings at Kells, and counts them again, and writes a letter to every abbot he knows.
endings.reward: Ten cows, about 300 d; flag bk_lost; shunned in every house of Columba's family for this generation, and cool for the next; the king of Brega's steward friendly

endings.how: The boat was chased in the North Channel and the chest went over the side, or was taken.
endings.text: Cellach hears it standing. He asks whether the men are alive, and then goes back to his building. The pages are painted again by other hands, more slowly.
endings.reward: flag bk_lost; no silver; Cellach cool but not an enemy, because the crew lived; a penance he may take at Tallaght to mend it

endings.how: He would not take the chest.
endings.text: The books go over in hide boats, three at a time, in the calm after Columba's feast. They arrive. Suibne says he could have told anyone they would.
endings.reward: Nothing lost and nothing gained; the story can be heard afterwards at the ford

stories.reward: A name in Columba's family of churches, which is a protector on every coast of this sea.

stories.title: A voice in the rows
stories.summary: In 871 two hundred ships come home from the rock on the Clyde with English, Britons and Picts, and captives are cheaper than hides. One of them calls to the merchant in a tongue he knows, and says his kin beyond the Tyne would pay.
stories.picture: A grey strand crowded with roped people in rows under a turf bank, long ships being unloaded behind, and in the front row a thin young man half risen, calling out to a merchant who has stopped walking.

beats.text: The fleet is in. Vemundr says the price is 'not the best' and means it has halved. A young man in the English row calls the merchant by the name of his boat's home.

beats.when: year >= 871 and year < 874 and not flag.duiblinn_osgar_bought
beats.text: He is Osgar, a reeve's son from north of the Tyne, taken with his lord's hostages on the rock. He can tally and read. Vemundr asks thirty pennies' weight and no haggling.
The ferryman's kin at the hurdles say there is a British girl in the same lot whom nobody has asked about, and that the saints' law forbids selling her at all.
The lord of the rock knows the family. The father is dead at York; an uncle holds the land and is slow to say whether he wants a nephew home.
At York the Danes hold the town. A man who can tally in two tongues is worth more here as a clerk than at home as an heir, and he knows it.
Vemundr has heard. He says only that a buyer who carries one home for nothing will be offered the next at a fair weight, and first.
Osgar chose the boat. His uncle the reeve sends down a cheese whenever the sail is seen, relieved, and ashamed of being relieved.

endings.how: The merchant bought Osgar and carried him north to his kin, asking only his cost.
endings.text: The uncle pays, grudging, and Osgar holds a strand north of the Tyne within three years. A keel of the house lands there without a gift from then on.
endings.reward: flag duiblinn_osgar_home; his cost back and about 120 d over; a landing beyond the Tyne with no gift owed; the English of the north friendly; Vemundr's first offer

endings.how: He bought Osgar and let him choose, and Osgar chose the boat.
endings.text: He sails with the house as its tally-man for nine years, reads every toll writ, and marries at Legacæstir. His son keeps the house's chest key after him.
endings.reward: A hand who reads Latin and English and reckons the northern weights (flag sv_scale if not yet set); toll men cheat the boat less; morale up among English hands

endings.how: He bought Osgar and the girl cheap and sold them where the price was whole.
endings.text: They fetch three times their cost in the east. The story goes up the English coast ahead of him, as stories do, with his boat's name in it.
endings.reward: About 180 d clear; deed bought_captives and deed sold_captives; cool among the English for a generation; Vemundr easy, neither better nor worse

endings.how: He walked on.
endings.text: The lot is sold by the new moon. Years later a clerk at York with a rope scar on his ankle reads the house's toll writ very slowly, twice.
endings.reward: Nothing; one toll at Eoforwic that takes a day longer than it should

stories.reward: A friend beyond the Tyne or a clerk in the boat, and the dealer's regard either way.

stories.title: The gate stands open
stories.summary: In 980 the Foreigners are beaten at Tara and the king of Tara shuts the town in for three days. When the gate opens every Irish slave walks out free, whatever was paid for them, and old King Amlaíb asks for a boat to Columba's island.
stories.picture: A town gate in an earth bank at first light, a tall Irish king on a horse beside it, and a long file of thin people walking out past him carrying nothing, while townsmen watch from the fence tops.

beats.text: Affraic says the king's sons are gone to Tara with every man who can carry a shield, and that anyone holding Irish hands on his plot should think what they will be worth by harvest.
The merchant has captives bought last week. The gate is shut and the smoke of the Irish camp is all round the bank. A buyer for Chester offers half, tonight, by boat.
On the fourth morning the gate opens. The king of Tara's steward stands at the landing and counts the Irish out of every hull, by name where he can get one.
Amlaíb Cuarán, baptised these forty years, gives up the kingship. He asks the merchant for passage to Hī, pays in advance with a ring, and brings one bag.
Abbot Mugrón meets the boat on the white strand. The old king walks up to the church without looking back at the sea. He dies there the same year or the next.
Sitriuc knows the house's name before it is said. He says: you carried my father. He says it in Irish, which is the tongue he keeps for things he means.

endings.how: The merchant took the old king to Hī and asked no more than the ring.
endings.text: The island buries him among kings. His son remembers it for forty years, and the house lies at the long stone without paying the king's man.
endings.reward: flag duiblinn_old_king_carried; a gold ring-pin worth about 200 d; no toll at Dyflin while Sitriuc lives; the abbot of Hī friendly; the tale told in the ale-house in both tongues

endings.how: He set his own Irish captives free inside the bank before the gate was opened.
endings.text: They walk out with the rest, and two of them say his name to the steward. The king of Tara's men search his boat last and lightly after that.
endings.reward: The loss of what he paid; the Irish of Leinster and Brega friendly at once; a protector's word inland; Affraic stands him a winter's ale

endings.how: He sold his captives to the Chester buyer in the dark, at half, before the gate opened.
endings.text: The boat slips out on the ebb. The steward learns the count was short and whose plot it was short on. He is patient about it.
endings.reward: Half his money back in silver; deed sold_captives; wary among the Irish for a generation; a fine of an ounce of silver when he next lands under an Irish king

endings.how: He would not carry Amlaíb.
endings.text: The old king goes in a hide boat with two monks. He arrives. Sitriuc is told who would not take his father, and is polite about it for forty years.
endings.reward: Nothing; the king's man at the landing weighs twice

stories.reward: A king's son who knows the house by name, or the goodwill of the Irish who walked out.

stories.title: An ounce on every plot
stories.summary: From 989 every plot in the town owes the king of Tara an ounce of gold each Christmas night, and gold is the one thing a town of silver-weighers has little of. A few years on the king wants pennies with his own name, and needs English ones to copy.
stories.picture: A snowy plank street at night, a steward with a torch and a small scale standing at a wattle gate, a householder weighing a twist of gold wire into the pan while the neighbours watch from their doors.

beats.text: On Christmas night the steward of the king of Tara walks the plank street with a scale. A plot that cannot weigh out its ounce of gold has its door marked.
Affraic says gold is to be had from a goldsmith at Chester and from men home from the east, and that the steward will take twelve ounces of clean silver if nobody is watching.
Sitriuc shows a penny of King Æthelred and asks for a bag of them, new and unclipped, from the mint on the Dee, and for word of a man there who can cut a die.
At the Dee the moneyers have Norse and Irish names and know very well what the pennies are wanted for. One will sell a worn die's pattern, if the reeve is not told.
The moneyer strikes the first bowl of pennies with the king's name. He hands the merchant one in ten of the first day's work and asks him to spend them abroad, loudly.
In the Danes' market a Dyflin penny goes on the scale with the rest, but the dealer turns it over first and asks where that king sits.

endings.how: The merchant brought the English pennies and the pattern, and spent the new coin abroad.
endings.text: Pennies with Sitriuc's name are taken at Chester and weighed at the Schlei. The king's man at the long stone takes the house's toll in coin at its face.
endings.reward: flag duiblinn_pennies_brought; one tenth of the first striking, about 150 d; change_coin at Dyflin without loss; Sitriuc friendly; the house's Christmas ounce paid from the king's own chest for three years

endings.how: He kept a plot and found the ounce of gold himself each year.
endings.text: The steward comes to know the door. In the third year he asks what else the house could carry inland, and to whom, under his lord's protection.
endings.reward: The plot kept; a protector's word from the king of Tara's steward, so the house may trade up the Boyne; costs an ounce of gold a year, about 300 d (?)

endings.how: He told the reeve at the Dee what the pennies were for.
endings.text: The reeve doubles the watch on the moneyers and thanks him with a writ. Sitriuc gets his pattern anyway, a year later, from Bristol, and remembers the delay.
endings.reward: Leave to come up the Dee without the forty-shilling fine; Sitriuc cool; no share in the striking

endings.how: He held a plot and did not pay.
endings.text: The door is marked at Christmas and the plot is another man's by Brigid's feast. Affraic keeps what was in the house until he comes for it.
endings.reward: The plot lost; his goods kept safe; nothing owed

stories.reward: The king's coin taken at its face, or an Irish steward's protection inland.

stories.title: The eldest of that kin
stories.summary: The men driven from the fort in 902 put what they could not carry into the ground by an English river, and none came back for it. The king's poet at Dyflin has the first of five questions from the giant's contest; the others lie at York, at sea and on Hī, and the answers lead to the bank of the Ribble.
stories.picture: A long hall by firelight, a stooped poet standing with a rune-cut stick held out across the fire toward a seated merchant, the benches behind them full of men who have stopped talking.

beats.text: The fort is empty and cattle graze in it. An old man at the hurdles, Norse by his father, says the hall's poet went to York with the old questions in his head, and that silver went into the ground by an English river.
The poet of the Norse kings at York sells the first question for ten pennies' weight: of what was the earth made, and the sky. He says the rest of the line is not all his to give.
Arnfinnr sells the first question here, or, if it is answered, gives the one that grows from it: how the giant begat children who had no wife. He asks what the merchant means to do at the end.
Arnfinnr says the men who taught him sat with men who knew an old Northman named Ravn, who set riddles to a Frisian house. He asks if the merchant has heard the name.
In the Wirral the children of the men of 902 farm and say nothing. One, hearing a verse of the giant's kin, finishes it, and then looks as if he wished he had not.
A brother on Hī, Norse-born and long baptised, has the last question: what the wise giant remembers first. The answer is a boat. He crosses himself after saying it.
The answers, laid end to end, are a road: from the flood, by a boat, to a south bank. A Wirral man, asked the right way, names the river: the Ribble, a day's walk up from the sea.
The poet is told the river. It was his fathers' silver, and he had thought a stranger would dig it. Men of the old families go with the merchant to the bank.

endings.how: The merchant answered all five and dug by the Ribble with his own men.
endings.text: There is more silver in the bank than the boat can lift: coin of York, of the Franks and of the caliphs, rings, and cut pieces. He takes what she will carry and covers the rest.
endings.reward: The riddle set's reward (riddles_793.json rw_hoard_cuerdale), as much as the hold bears; deed won_great_riddle; flag rd_setter_known; Arnfinnr wary when he hears, since it was his fathers' silver

endings.how: He told Arnfinnr the place and dug with the heirs of the men of 902.
endings.text: The king's ships fetch it in one night. The merchant's share is a tenth and a plot on the plank street, and the poet makes a verse with a Frisian in it.
endings.reward: A tenth of the silver; a plot at Dyflin free of the king's share; deed won_great_riddle; flag rd_setter_known; Arnfinnr a fast friend, and his word in the hall at York

endings.how: He told the English king's reeve at Legacæstir.
endings.text: The reeve's men dig it for their lord. The merchant has a writ for the Dee and a finder's part, and a name among the Wirral men that he would rather not have.
endings.reward: A finder's part, about a twentieth; leave to come up the Dee; the English of Mercia friendly; the Norse of Dyflin and the Wirral wary for a generation

endings.how: He learned the place and left it in the ground.
endings.text: Nobody digs. The river goes on cutting its bank. A thousand years later it will be found by men mending the same bank, which is the true end of it.
endings.reward: Nothing but the knowledge, which an heir inherits with the chest; Arnfinnr says it was the right answer to a sixth question he had not asked

stories.reward: The silver of the men of 902, or the friendship of their heirs.

works.name: New hurdles for the ford
works.what: The woven hazel hurdles that give the ford its name are pegged down afresh from bank to bank after a winter flood, with a row of stakes upstream to break the current.
works.needs: The ferryman's goodwill, low water at a spring tide, and hazel cut in the hills, which a king's steward must allow.
works.gives: Carts come down to the strand at any ebb, so loading here takes a day less; crossing costs the house nothing; the ferryman's kin friendly, and remembered by their heirs.
works.picture: Men and boys knee-deep in a brown river at low water, pegging pale new wattle panels onto the bed with mallets, a punt alongside loaded with hazel rods.
works.source: Áth Cliath, the ford of hurdles: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Dublin_to_795. That the hurdles needed relaying is inference; the tale that they were first laid for a Leinster king is late (?)

works.name: A bell for the church by the pool
works.what: A hand-bell of folded sheet iron, riveted and dipped in bronze, such as every church of the Irish has on its altar sill, to replace one that is cracked.
works.needs: To be the steward's guest; bar iron and a little copper and tin brought in, since none is made here.
works.gives: The house's name said at Mass on Brigid's feast; sanctuary in the ring for its men; the steward stands surety for it without a gift from then on.
works.picture: A smith by a charcoal pit lowering a squared iron hand-bell on tongs into a clay mould glowing with bronze, a grey-haired steward and a boy watching from the church bank.
works.source: Irish iron hand-bells coated in bronze, of the 8th and 9th centuries (C. Bourke's studies, from memory (?)). Oaths were sworn on a saint's bell: peoples/irish_gaelic.md

works.name: A house on your plot
works.what: A post-and-wattle house of the town's kind on a fenced plot by the plank street: four roof posts, a hearth in the middle, a bench down each side, a store pit, and a path of split logs to the gate.
works.needs: A plot bought from the king's man; hazel and ash from the Irish side; from 989 the ounce of gold each Christmas night.
works.gives: Free lodging and a dry store for the house's goods in the town; a door for news and a place to leave a factor; the plot is rebuilt on the same fence line after every fire.
works.picture: Men weaving hazel rods between upright posts on a narrow fenced strip, a roof frame half thatched, plank path in front and the river behind, a child carrying clay in a basket.
works.source: The houses and fourteen plots of Fishamble Street, rebuilt on the same lines some thirteen times: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wood_Quay; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Scandinavian_Dublin. The Christmas gold: Annals of Tigernach 989

works.name: A length of the town bank
works.what: Twenty paces of the earth bank that is being thrown up round the town, faced with wattle and topped with a fence of split oak, built at the house's cost on the river side.
works.needs: The king's leave, a plot or a store in the town, and men to dig between hay and harvest.
works.gives: A berth under the bank at the long stone that is the house's own; the king's man takes a tenth less of its loads; a voice at the law mound as a man who built.
works.picture: A line of diggers with wooden spades piling dark clay against a wattle face along a river strand, ships drawn up below them, a man driving split oak pales into the top.
works.source: The earth bank of about 950 at Wood Quay: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wood_Quay. The town was burned in 944 (Annals of Ulster). That townsmen built it in lengths is the game's guess (?)

works.name: A roof beam for Holy Trinity
works.what: A squared oak tie-beam for the king's new wooden church on the height, carried up from the yard on rollers, with the giver's mark cut where only the wrights will see it.
works.needs: The bishop's leave and the shipwright's best oak, which he gives up unwillingly.
works.gives: The house's dead prayed for by name at the Trinity; sanctuary there; Bishop Dúnán's letter of good word to Canterbury, which opens church doors in England.
works.picture: A dozen men hauling a long squared oak beam uphill on rollers through a town of thatched roofs toward a half-built wooden church, a bishop in a plain cloak walking beside it.
works.source: Holy Trinity, founded soon after 1028, of wood, its bishop answering for a time to Canterbury: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christ_Church_Cathedral,_Dublin. The beam is the game's

ships.how: built to order in a month
ships.note: A frame of hazel and ash covered with tanned ox-hides sewn and greased, with a mast and a small sail. Hides are the one thing this shore always has. Light enough for four men to carry up the strand, and she goes where the ford stops a keel.
ships.picture: A long hide boat upside down on trestles by a wattle house, two men sewing a seam with a bone needle, a pot of grease beside them.
ships.source: Ships.md (curuca, curach); peoples/irish_gaelic.md, section 6; the pilgrims' boat of two hides and a half, Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 891 (Ingram 1823)

ships.note: A dugout of one oak, used at the ford and on the river above it for cattle fodder, turf and eels. The ferryman's kin always know of one for sale.
ships.picture: A dark hollowed log boat half full of cut turf, nosed into reeds beside a line of hurdles in a brown river.
ships.source: Ships.md: the game's table has Irish finds of logboats; none is recorded at this ford (?)

ships.note: A ship's boat or a four-oar boat off the strand below the fort, sold by men who have more hulls than hands after a bad summer.
ships.picture: A small clinker boat with a curled stem pulled up on sand beside a much larger hull, a man knocking a rivet home.
ships.source: The ship-fort of 841 and the fleets of 849 and 871: dossier, section 5. That boats were sold is the game's

ships.how: built to order in six weeks
ships.note: The yard turns these out between larger orders, of Irish oak, for fishing the bay and for lightering casks to the plank street.
ships.picture: Three small new clinker boats in a row on a strand, pale and untarred, under the stern of a great ship on blocks.
ships.source: Shipwrights among the town's crafts (dossier, section 3 (?)); toy boats of the same lines from Wood Quay

ships.how: built to order over a winter
ships.note: A sailing and rowing ship of twelve to eighteen paces, the working hull of the Irish Sea: she carries hides and people out and wine and salt home, and is what the town sells to Chester, Bristol and the Isles.
ships.picture: A broad clinker ship on rollers with her mast stepped and a striped sail bent on, men carrying hides up a plank into her.
ships.source: Ships are among the town's exports, 917 to 1066: dossier, section 4; Design/content/realms/irish_sea.md

ships.how: built to order over two winters, with the king's leave
ships.note: The yard can build the largest warship on this sea, sixty oars and thirty paces. No king lets a merchant have one for the asking; it is ordered for a lord, and the merchant finds the oak, the iron and the silver.
ships.picture: An immense slender hull on blocks along a strand at low sun, sixty oar ports down her side, a shipwright the size of an ant walking her keel.
ships.source: Skuldelev 2, built in the Dublin area about 1042: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skuldelev_ships

sayings.text: Three sounds of increase: the lowing of a cow in milk; the din of a smithy; the swish of a plough.
sayings.source: The Triads of Ireland, tr. Kuno Meyer (1906; Meyer died 1919), as given in Design/content/peoples/irish_gaelic.md

sayings.text: Three false sisters: 'perhaps,' 'may be,' 'I dare say.'
sayings.source: The Triads of Ireland, tr. Kuno Meyer (1906), as given in peoples/irish_gaelic.md

sayings.text: Three signs of ill-breeding: a long visit, staring, constant questioning.
