sayings.source: The Triads of Ireland, tr. Kuno Meyer (1906), as given in peoples/irish_gaelic.md. Said at the guest-house to a merchant who has done all three

sayings.text: Máel Ruain: 'the liquor that causes forgetfulness of God shall not be drunk here.' Dublitir of Finglas: 'my monks shall drink it, and they shall be in Heaven along with thine.'
sayings.source: The Monastery of Tallaght 6, tr. E. J. Gwynn and W. J. Purton (1911; Gwynn died 1941; Purton's death year not checked (?)), as given in peoples/irish_gaelic.md. Two abbots a morning's walk from the pool, both dead by 796

sayings.text: New parchment, bad ink. O I say nothing more.
sayings.source: A scribe's marginal note, about 850: Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus II, ed. Stokes and Strachan (1903), as given in peoples/irish_gaelic.md

sayings.text: Bitter is the wind to-night, / It tosses the ocean's white hair: / To-night I fear not the fierce warriors of Norway / Coursing on the Irish Sea.
sayings.source: texts_793.json irish_viking_terror (tr. Kuno Meyer, Selections from Ancient Irish Poetry, 1911). A margin verse of about 850: not for a mouth before the fleets

sayings.text: Forth shall one go, nor stay as a guest in a single spot forever; love becomes loathing if long one sits by the hearth in another's home.
sayings.source: Hávamál 35, tr. Henry Adams Bellows (1923): texts_793.json havamal_035, set here as prose. Said in the fort to a merchant in his third week

sayings.text: Until you have a host you are a grey dog. After, you are his dog, which is better fed.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner, on the law's word for a stranger from over the sea, cú glas (peoples/irish_gaelic.md, after Kelly)

sayings.text: A king named for his sandal, a king named for his beard. In Dyflin they look a man up and down before they obey him.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner: Amlaíb Cuarán, 'sandal', and Sitriuc Silkbeard (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amla%C3%ADb_Cuar%C3%A1n; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigtrygg_Silkbeard)

sayings.text: The Irish kept the ford and the Northmen took the pool, and each calls the whole place by his half.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner: Áth Cliath and Dyflin, from Duiblinn (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Dublin)

sayings.text: In the year of the siege a man offered his neighbour a drink and was asked: which tide?
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner, a Northman's understatement: the besieged had no water but sea water in 989 (Annals of Tigernach, via realms/irish_sea.md)

easter_eggs.text: Children on the plank street sail small wooden boats in the gutter, carved with a proper stem and a hole for a mast. One is cut on the lines of a boat far too small and old for this town.
easter_eggs.source: Toy boats from the Wood Quay digs: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wood_Quay. The likeness to the house's Gislinge boat is the game's

easter_eggs.text: A grave by the weir holds a folding bronze scale and a set of lead weights beside the sword. The dead man's kin say he was as proud of the one as of the other.
easter_eggs.source: Folding scales and weights among the grave goods at Kilmainham and Islandbridge: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilmainham (dossier, from memory (?))

easter_eggs.text: Five young men lie buried by the pool with their weapons. Two grew up in the north and two somewhere in these islands; the fifth nobody could say.
easter_eggs.source: The warrior burials at Ship Street Great and South Great George's Street, 9th century, with the isotope results: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Scandinavian_Dublin. Seen in the game from 841

easter_eggs.text: The great ship on the blocks in the yard about 1042 will end her days sunk on purpose across a channel in a Danish fjord, a long way from this strand, and be lifted out nine hundred years later.
easter_eggs.source: Skuldelev 2: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skuldelev_ships. Nobody in the game can know it; it is in the picture's note, not in a mouth

easter_eggs.text: A moneyer at Chester under King Edward signs his pennies Irfara: the Ireland-farer. The skippers of Dyflin ask after him by that name long after he is dead.
easter_eggs.source: The moneyer Irfara at Chester: Victoria County History of Chester, via dossiers/legacaestir.md

easter_eggs.text: The Irish say that the best pilot in the west of the world was a merchant of the Isle of Man named Manannán, who knew by the sky how long fair weather would last, and that men called him a god of the sea for it.
easter_eggs.source: Cormac's Glossary, about 900, tr. O'Donovan, ed. Stokes (1868), as given in peoples/irish_gaelic.md, section 4. Not for a mouth before 900

easter_eggs.text: On the morning of the battle of 1014 the tide was full at about sunrise and full again at about sunset, so that in the evening the water lay between the beaten men and their ships.
easter_eggs.source: The tide was reckoned in 1860 and matches the tale: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Clontarf. The tale is of the 12th century, not the annals

easter_eggs.text: A stick of yew with runes cut on it lies in the mud of a plot by the river. It says who owned it and nothing else.
easter_eggs.source: Runes on wood and bone from Wood Quay: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wood_Quay (what they say is the game's (?))

easter_eggs.text: The old people at the ford say the pool is named for a woman called Dub who was drowned in it by a jealous wife's spell. The monks at Tallaght say it is named for being black.
easter_eggs.source: The place-lore tale of Dub, known to the dossier only from memory (?); the name means black pool (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Dublin_to_795)

unlocks.what: The steward's protection: a host at the black pool
unlocks.how: Before 841, bring Tipraite or his heir a gift of wine or salt and let him take first choice of the cargo, twice.
unlocks.gives: flag duiblinn_guest: the market opens at the guest-house with sureties found; lodging free; an honour-price in Leinster for a season, so a wrong done to the house can be sued for.

unlocks.what: The ferryman's marks for the bar
unlocks.how: Hire Suibne as pilot three times, or pay for the new hurdles at the ford.
unlocks.gives: The house's ships cross the bar at any state of the tide without a pilot; hire_pilot here costs nothing; the knowledge passes to the heirs, and the ferryman's kin tell it back to them in every later age.

unlocks.how: Before 824, bring Óengus the name and day of a saint from three churches over the sea (Traiectum, Lindisfarena and one Frankish house will do), or a bundle of calfskin and a measure of oak galls.
unlocks.gives: flag bk_parchment; deed gave_alms; he reads and writes Latin letters for the house without fee; one text copied for the chest at Tallaght (copy_text) each visit.

unlocks.how: Between 845 and 880, sell him grain or wine in two winters running and weigh with your own scale.
unlocks.gives: flag sv_scale if not yet set; goods on the strand of the captives are offered to the house before the fleet's own buyers, at the first weight named.

unlocks.what: The first question of the giant's line
unlocks.how: From 917, buy it from Arnfinnr in the king's hall for ten pennies' weight of silver, or win a riddle from him first and have it for nothing.
unlocks.gives: give_riddle r-vafth-20; the set ymirs_kin opens, with its next questions at Eoforwic, at sea and at Hī.

unlocks.what: No toll at the long stone
unlocks.how: Carry old King Amlaíb to Hī in 980, or bring Sitriuc his English pennies after 995.
unlocks.gives: The king's man takes nothing from the house's loads at Dyflin while Sitriuc lives (to 1036); his heirs take half.

unlocks.what: The Sunday rule, learned and not paid for
unlocks.how: After 980, ask the law at the mound or listen to Affraic before loading on a Saturday evening.
unlocks.gives: law: no loading, selling or travelling from Saturday evening to Monday morning under an Irish king; a merchant who knows it is not fined an ounce of silver and his load is not forfeited.

unlocks.what: A plot on the plank street
unlocks.how: From 917, buy it from the king's man (buy_plot), or be given it for sharing the silver by the Ribble.
unlocks.gives: The work 'A house on your plot' opens; rent_store is free; from 989 the plot owes an ounce of gold each Christmas night.

unlocks.what: The strake with the house's mark
unlocks.how: From 1028, let Asgrimr haul the house's oldest boat and look underneath, and buy or order one hull from the yard.
unlocks.gives: Repairs at the yard at cost and done first; one fit_upgrade without waiting; the wright's word on any hull the house thinks of buying anywhere on this sea.
